title: LLM Grounding
body:
**Grounding** supplies a language model with the specific facts it should answer from, sent
alongside the question, so its response describes the actual situation in front of the user,
and its training data stops being the source.

The problem it solves is concrete. Asked about a stock's risk, an ungrounded model answers from
training data, which is generic, possibly years stale, and unconnected to the date range and
figures the user is looking at. It will also produce a confident number that is wrong, because
producing plausible text is what it does.

The project's approach is a context builder: every computed statistic is formatted into a
plain-text block and included with each request.

```
build_stock_context(ticker, company_name, start_date, end_date,
                    period_return_pct, ann_vol_pct, sharpe_ratio,
                    avg_daily_move_pct, best_day_pct, worst_day_pct,
                    trading_days)
```

The model then explains numbers it was handed, with no recall of training data involved, which
changes its role from an oracle to an interpreter and is what makes the panel trustworthy
enough to ship.

Three engineering decisions surround it, and each is about a failure mode of the system around
the model:

```
per-session call limit    caps cost and abuse, since the endpoint is public
key from the environment  the API key stays off the client and out of the repository
system prompt             fixes the role, constrains the tone, and refuses to
                          give financial advice
```

The last is a liability decision expressed as a prompt, which is the kind of requirement
[[INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY AND SOCIETY]] examines. The pure-Python context builder
is also the part of the system that unit tests can exercise with no network and no framework,
which is why it was written with no dependencies.
